newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia gov't holds out olive branch to rebels.
newsitem.headline: Colombia gov't holds out olive branch to rebels.

text.p: The Colombian government called on Friday for unconditional peace talks with the country's leftist guerrillas and said it recognised them as a legitimate political force that has to be reckoned with.

The dramatic move came a day after President Ernesto Samper's new defence minister, civilian business leader Gilberto Echeverri Mejia, was sworn in and vowed to make the pursuit of peace his top priority.

Powerful military leaders and right-wing politicians have long derided Colombia's two leading rebel groups as little more than heavily-armed bandits and "narco-guerrillas" working in league with the country's drug gangs.

But in a statement on Friday, the government called them "valid political interlocutors" and said it trusted their leaders were people with whom it was possible "to open a frank and transparent negotiating process."

When Samper unveiled a peace plan in May 1995, the veteran heads of Colombia's Marxist-led guerrilla groups responded with a bloody offensive in which more than 150 people were reported killed and hundreds injured.
Nearly two years later, the government clearly believes that times have changed.
The statement recognising the groups came in an eight-point "agenda for peace" that the government drafted for talks with academics, church and business leaders and politicians.
The closed-door meeting in the small town of Altos de Yerbabuena on the northern outskirts of Bogota could mark a turning point in the conflict that has racked Colombia since the mid-1960s.

The first point on the agenda, "Recognition of the political character of the armed conflict and guerrilla organisations," flew in the face of persistent military efforts to depict rebels as gangsters devoid of any political beliefs or ideology.
It said the insurgents had legitimate political aspirations that should ultimately be accommodated as part of a broader Colombian democracy.

It also urged the Revoltuonary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and National Liberation Army (ELN) to consider the challenge of winning their long-running struggle for power with ballots instead of bullets.
"The government does not intend either to object to the political model of the guerrillas or to achieve their surrender through negotiations," the statement said.

Instead, it said, it was seeking to pave the way for rebels "to freely submit their plans and programmes to national scrutiny so that they can legitimately aspire to become a true alternative for power without the use of arms."

In a possible stumbling block to peace talks, the statement said no pre-conditions were acceptable for face-to-face talks to end a war that dates back more than three decades and has taken tens of thousands of lives.

The army has balked in the past at rebel demands for the demilitarization of vast tracts of national territory as a condition for negotiations. The government said no calls for cease-fires or a suspension of military activity would be accepted as a pre-condition for talks.
